turns.doctor_question: Hello, please have a seat. What brings you into the clinic today?
turns.patient_response:
Hi, thanks. Um, so I guess what finally made me come in is that I just... I keep turning in these job applications, or like, my research notes, and they always have these small but really embarrassing mistakes on them. Like I'll mislabel an artwork date. Which is so frustrating because I spent four years studying this stuff, mostly focusing on 19th-century realism, which is fascinating—Courbet is probably my favorite, though my roommate hates him because he thinks the colors are too drab. We actually got into a huge argument about it last week when we were trying to pick a poster for the living room, and we ended up just getting this weird vintage movie poster instead. 

But, right, anyway... I’ll mess up a date like that, or I'll just completely skip a question on a form, even when I honestly thought I had checked the whole thing over. It keeps happening, and it's just... yeah, it's not great.

symptom_reasoning.S001: The patient explicitly states they make small, embarrassing mistakes on applications and notes, such as mislabeling dates or skipping questions despite checking them over.

turns.doctor_question: Have you noticed these kinds of careless mistakes and attention issues ever since you were a child, or did this start more recently?
turns.patient_response: Yeah, it's... it's definitely been a thing for a long time. Even back in elementary school, my teachers would always write on my report cards that I had really good ideas, but I'd forget to turn in worksheets, or I'd lose the instructions for a project. Or I'd just miss all these little details unless my parents checked my backpack every single night. Which they hated doing, by the way. My mom is this super organized person, like, she color-codes her spice rack. I tried doing that once in my apartment, but I got halfway through the alphabet and then I found this old jar of star anise that I bought for a recipe I never made, and I ended up spending like two hours watching YouTube videos about how star anise is harvested in Vietnam. It's actually really interesting, they grow on these evergreen trees... but yeah, anyway, my parents had to check my backpack all the time because I'd just lose things or mess up the details. So, yeah, it's not new.

symptom_reasoning.S001: The patient explicitly mentions missing little details and messing up details since childhood.
symptom_reasoning.S004: The patient describes failing to follow through on schoolwork by forgetting to turn in worksheets.
symptom_reasoning.S007: The patient reports a history of losing things, such as project instructions, requiring their parents to check their backpack.
symptom_reasoning.S008: The patient demonstrates distractibility by describing how they abandoned organizing a spice rack to spend two hours watching unrelated YouTube videos about star anise.

turns.doctor_question: Do you find yourself constantly worrying about many different everyday things, to the point where it feels difficult to control?
turns.patient_response: Um, no, not really. I mean, I don't think I worry more than anyone else. Like, I'll stress out about a job interview, sure, but it's not like this constant, uncontrollable thing. Actually, speaking of interviews, I had one last week for this gallery assistant position, and the guy interviewing me had the most incredible collection of antique pocket watches on his desk. I asked him about one, and it turned out it was a Waltham from like, 1908. Which is wild because Waltham was actually a huge deal in the American industrial revolution. They pioneered this system of interchangeable parts for watches, which totally changed manufacturing. Henry Ford even visited their factory before he set up his assembly line. So we ended up talking about that for like twenty minutes, which was great, but then I realized we barely talked about the actual job. I haven't heard back yet, so I'm a little bummed about that, but... wait, what were you asking? Oh, right, worrying. Yeah, no, I don't really have that issue. Just the normal stuff, I guess.

symptom_reasoning.S008: The patient becomes distracted by their own unrelated thoughts about pocket watches and loses track of the doctor's question.
symptom_reasoning.S015: The patient talks excessively, going on a long, unprompted tangent about the history of pocket watches.
symptom_reasoning.S056: The patient explicitly denies worrying more than anyone else or experiencing constant worry.
symptom_reasoning.S057: The patient explicitly denies that their worry is an 'uncontrollable thing'.
